questions.stem: Which problem faced the Chinese Republic in 1927?
options: A communist government ruled from Beijing and was recognised by the Western powers
Much of the country was controlled by rival warlords with their own armies
Japan had already annexed all of northern China and set up a puppet emperor in Beijing
The Qing dynasty had returned to power and controlled most of the southern provinces
questions.explanation: After Yuan Shikai's death in 1916, power fragmented among warlords, and the government in Beijing had little real authority. Japan's seizure of Manchuria came in 1931, and Puyi became head of Manchukuo in 1932.

questions.stem: Foreign 'concessions' and extraterritoriality angered Chinese nationalists in the 1920s because they:
options: banned Chinese people from trading with any foreign country except Japan and Britain
gave foreign missionaries the right to appoint the governors of the coastal provinces
let foreigners live under their own laws in Chinese cities, beyond Chinese courts
forced Chinese citizens to pay all of their taxes directly to the British government
questions.explanation: Under the 'unequal treaties', foreigners in concessions such as Shanghai's International Settlement were tried by their own consuls, and foreign powers also controlled China's tariffs. Ending these privileges was a key nationalist aim.

questions.stem: Most Chinese people in the late 1920s were peasants whose main grievances were:
options: the forced collectivisation of their family farms
the closure of village schools by the Nationalists
high rents, debt, heavy taxes and landlord power
the loss of their votes in national elections
questions.explanation: Peasants often paid half or more of their harvest in rent and suffered from debt, warlord taxes and natural disasters. China had no national elections in which peasants voted, and collectivisation came only under the communists in the 1950s.

questions.stem: Who commanded the National Revolutionary Army on the Northern Expedition of 1926-1928?
options: the warlord Zhang Zuolin of Manchuria
Sun Yixian, who died in Nanjing in 1928
Jiang Jieshi (Chiang Kai-shek)
Mao Zedong and Zhu De together
questions.explanation: Jiang commanded the National Revolutionary Army, which advanced north to defeat or win over the warlords. Sun Yixian had died in Beijing in 1925, and Zhang Zuolin was one of the warlords the expedition opposed.

questions.stem: What was the impact of the Northern Expedition by the end of 1928?
options: Japan withdrew from Manchuria and gave up its rights in China in return for recognition
China was nominally united under a Nationalist government in Nanjing, but many warlords kept their armies
China was fully united and every warlord had been defeated, disarmed and removed from power
The communists controlled Beijing and Nanjing and shared power equally with the Nationalists
questions.explanation: Beijing fell in June 1928 and the Manchurian leader Zhang Xueliang accepted Nanjing's authority in December. But many warlords joined the Nationalists only in name and kept their own forces, and the CCP had been purged in 1927.

questions.stem: The Shanghai Massacre of April 1927 changed Chinese politics mainly because it:
options: brought the CCP into the Nationalist government as equal partners in a new coalition
led the Western powers to give up their concessions and leave Shanghai within a year
made Mao Zedong the leader of the KMT after Jiang Jieshi was forced to resign in disgrace
ended the First United Front and drove the CCP out of the cities into the countryside
questions.explanation: Jiang's purge of communists and union activists, aided by the Green Gang, broke the alliance with the CCP. Communist uprisings later in 1927 failed, and the survivors retreated to rural bases such as Jinggangshan.

questions.stem: Which was an achievement of the Nationalist Government in Nanjing between 1928 and 1937?
options: holding free national elections in which several parties competed for power
recovering control of China's tariffs and building new roads and railways
carrying out a full land reform that gave every tenant farmer their own land
defeating Japan in Manchuria and recovering the province by 1933
questions.explanation: The Nationalists regained tariff autonomy by 1930, built roads and railways, reformed the currency in 1935 and modernised parts of the army with German advisers. They did not carry out land reform, lost Manchuria to Japan, and ruled as a one-party state.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the Nationalist Government's base of support was too narrow. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: It gave too much power to the peasants, so landlords and businessmen withdrew their support
It allowed free elections, so its opponents were able to win control of the parliament in 1931
It relied on landlords, the army and urban business, and left peasant grievances such as rents unaddressed
It was supported by every warlord, the CCP and the peasants but it lost the backing of all the Western powers
questions.explanation: The Nationalists depended on the army, rural elites and Shanghai business and banking circles, and a 1930 law limiting rents was barely enforced. Most of the population, the peasants, gained little from Nationalist rule, which later helped the CCP.

questions.stem: Jiang Jieshi's 'encirclement campaigns' of 1930-1934 were aimed at:
options: destroying the communist base areas, especially the Jiangxi Soviet
driving the Japanese army out of the provinces of Manchuria
forcing the foreign powers to leave their concessions in Shanghai and Tianjin
defeating the warlord Feng Yuxiang in the Central Plains War
questions.explanation: Five campaigns were launched against the communist bases. The fifth, using a blockhouse strategy on German advice, forced the CCP to abandon Jiangxi in October 1934. The Central Plains War of 1930 was a separate conflict with rival warlords.

questions.stem: How did Mao Zedong's view of revolution in the late 1920s differ from the Comintern's advice to the CCP?
options: Mao wanted to seize the big cities at once, while the Comintern preferred rural bases
Mao saw the peasants as the main revolutionary force, while the Comintern stressed urban workers
Mao wanted to cooperate with Jiang Jieshi forever, while the Comintern demanded a split
Mao rejected Marxism entirely, while the Comintern asked the CCP to become nationalist
questions.explanation: Following Soviet doctrine, the Comintern and leaders such as Li Lisan pushed for urban uprisings, which failed, as at Changsha in 1930. Mao built rural bases and a peasant army, which became the basis of the CCP's success.

questions.stem: After the failure of the Autumn Harvest Uprising, Mao and Zhu De built the Red Army in a base at:
options: the Jinggang Mountains, on the Hunan-Jiangxi border
Shanghai's International Settlement and the docks
Nanjing, the capital of the Nationalist Government
Manchuria, close to the border with the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: In 1928 Mao and Zhu De combined their forces at Jinggangshan, the base from which they later moved to set up the Jiangxi Soviet. The cities were dangerous for communists after 1927.

questions.stem: At the Zunyi Conference of January 1935, Mao's position improved because:
options: the leaders who had directed the defeat in Jiangxi, including Bo Gu and Otto Braun, were criticised
Jiang Jieshi agreed to recognise Mao as the head of a separate communist state in the north
the Comintern sent an order from Moscow naming Mao as the sole and permanent leader of the whole party
the CCP voted to abandon Marxism and adopt Mao's own Three Principles of the People
questions.explanation: The conference blamed Bo Gu and the Comintern adviser Otto Braun for using positional warfare against the fifth encirclement, and Mao gained a leading role in military affairs. He consolidated full control of the party later, during the Yan'an period.

questions.stem: The 'mass line' in CCP practice required party members to:
options: follow every instruction from Moscow without consulting the peasants or local cadres
avoid all contact with the peasants so the party's plans could be kept completely secret
allow peasants to elect the Central Committee in open and competitive party elections
learn the people's concerns and turn them into policies explained back to the people
questions.explanation: The mass line, 'from the masses, to the masses', meant gathering ideas from ordinary people, shaping them into policy and taking it back for action. It built peasant trust while keeping decisions in the party's hands.

questions.stem: In On New Democracy (1940), Mao argued that after victory China would first have:
options: a coalition of revolutionary classes led by the CCP, before moving to socialism
a capitalist democracy with free elections and no special role for the CCP at all
an immediate Soviet-style economy with all land and factories owned by the state
a restored constitutional monarchy with the last emperor Puyi as head of state
questions.explanation: New Democracy promised an alliance of workers, peasants, petty bourgeoisie and national bourgeoisie under communist leadership. This moderate program reassured many non-communists in the 1940s.

questions.stem: By 1945 the CCP's Seventh Congress wrote 'Mao Zedong Thought' into the party constitution. This shows the development of CCP ideology because it:
options: placed the CCP under the direct command of Stalin and the Soviet Communist Party
committed the CCP to the urban insurrection strategy of the early Comintern years
marked Marxism-Leninism adapted to Chinese conditions, with Mao as its authority
ended the party's commitment to Marxism and replaced it with Confucian principles
questions.explanation: The 'sinification' of Marxism stressed peasant revolution, rural bases and the mass line. Naming Mao Zedong Thought as the party's guide confirmed both an independent Chinese line and Mao's personal authority.

questions.stem: The Long March of 1934-1935 began in Jiangxi and ended in:
options: Shanghai, at the mouth of the Yangtze
Manchuria, near the Soviet border
northern Shaanxi, in north-west China
Guangzhou, on the southern coast
questions.explanation: The Central Red Army left Jiangxi in October 1934 and reached northern Shaanxi in October 1935, later making its base at Yan'an. The route took it west and north through some of China's hardest terrain.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Long March is accurate?
options: The march was completed in a few weeks with very little fighting at all
Only a small fraction of the soldiers who left Jiangxi reached the north
Most of the soldiers who left Jiangxi arrived safely in the north in 1935
The marchers travelled mostly by railway to avoid the Nationalist armies
questions.explanation: Battles, desertion, disease and the hardships of mountains and grasslands reduced the army dramatically; tens of thousands set out and only a few thousand of them arrived. Exact figures and the total distance vary between sources.

questions.stem: Historians argue that the Long March was a military defeat but a political victory for the CCP. Which consequence best supports the 'political victory' view?
options: It led the Soviet Union to send large armies to defend the new northern base
It confirmed Mao's leadership and became a heroic legend used in CCP propaganda
It destroyed the Nationalist army, which never again fought the Red Army in battle
It persuaded Japan to withdraw from Manchuria and seek peace with the communists
questions.explanation: The march established Mao's leadership, spread the CCP's message to the areas it passed through, and created a story of endurance used ever after. The Nationalists remained much stronger militarily, and Japan kept advancing.

questions.stem: The Mukden Incident of September 1931 led to:
options: Japan's seizure of Manchuria and the creation of Manchukuo
the Second United Front between the KMT and the CCP
the start of the Long March from the Jiangxi Soviet
the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor and war with the United States
questions.explanation: The Kwantung Army staged an explosion on a railway near Mukden as a pretext and occupied Manchuria, creating the puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932. The Second United Front came only after the Xi'an Incident of December 1936.

questions.stem: Full-scale war between China and Japan began after a clash in July 1937 at:
options: the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing
the Lugou railway station in Nanjing
the Shanghai Bund near the Huangpu
the Mukden railway near Shenyang
questions.explanation: The Marco Polo (Lugou) Bridge Incident of 7 July 1937 escalated into the Second Sino-Japanese War. Japan captured Shanghai and Nanjing later in 1937. The Mukden Incident was the 1931 pretext for seizing Manchuria.

questions.stem: What was the main economic impact of the Japanese advance of 1937-1938 on the Nationalist Government?
options: It lost the coastal cities, industry and customs revenue, and paid for the war by printing money
It gained new industrial cities in the west, which made it richer than before the war began
It was able to raise taxes on the coastal cities, which remained under its control until 1945
It received so much Soviet aid that it no longer needed any revenue from taxes or trade
questions.explanation: With Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan and Guangzhou lost by late 1938, the government retreated to Chongqing, cut off from its main revenue. Printing money caused severe inflation that ruined salaried workers and soldiers.

questions.stem: In June 1938 Nationalist forces broke the dykes of the Yellow River. This shows the impact of the war on Chinese civilians because:
options: it ended the war in northern China and allowed refugees to return home in the following year
it was a small local event that affected only a few villages near the river mouth on the coast
it slowed the Japanese advance but flooded vast areas, killing many civilians and creating millions of refugees
it was carried out by the Japanese army to punish villages that had supported communist guerrillas
questions.explanation: The deliberate breach at Huayuankou delayed Japan's advance towards Wuhan, but the floods killed large numbers of people and displaced millions. Estimates of the deaths vary widely, so historians cite ranges.

questions.stem: Why did the CCP's Hundred Regiments Offensive of 1940 matter for its later wartime strategy?
options: it was a joint offensive with the KMT that restored the United Front for the rest of the war
it drove Japan out of northern China, so the CCP no longer needed to fight in the region
Japan's harsh retaliation led the CCP to avoid large battles and rely on guerrilla warfare
its complete success persuaded the CCP to fight only large conventional battles after 1940
questions.explanation: The offensive, led by Peng Dehuai, damaged Japanese railways and posts but provoked ferocious 'Three Alls' reprisals against communist areas. Afterwards the CCP concentrated on guerrilla tactics and building bases.

questions.stem: Which comparison best describes the differing strategies of the KMT and CCP towards Japan from 1939?
options: The KMT traded space for time and preserved its forces; the CCP expanded rural bases behind Japanese lines
The KMT fought only guerrilla actions; the CCP fought most of the large conventional battles of the whole war
The KMT surrendered to Japan in 1939; the CCP fought on alone with large-scale help from the USA
The KMT and the CCP merged their armies under a single command led by Mao from 1939 to 1945
questions.explanation: After 1938 Jiang retreated to Chongqing, avoided heavy losses and waited for foreign help, while the CCP grew its armies and base areas through guerrilla warfare and mobilising peasants. The KMT fought most of the big battles, and the two sides remained rivals.

questions.stem: The New Fourth Army Incident of January 1941 was significant because:
options: Mao was captured by Nationalist troops and held prisoner until the end of the war
Nationalist troops attacked a communist army, effectively ending cooperation in the United Front
the CCP and KMT armies jointly defeated a major Japanese force in central China
the USA agreed to arm the communist New Fourth Army instead of the Nationalists
questions.explanation: Nationalist forces ambushed the communist New Fourth Army in Anhui, killing or capturing thousands. The United Front survived in name, but each side increasingly prepared for a showdown after the war.

questions.stem: The American general Joseph Stilwell clashed with Jiang Jieshi until Stilwell's recall in 1944. Their dispute illustrates which criticism of Jiang's wartime leadership?
options: that he refused all American aid and relied only on Soviet weapons and advisers
that he held back his best troops from fighting Japan to save them for war with the CCP
that he spent too heavily on attacking Japan and left China with no army for the future
that he allowed the CCP too much influence in the government in Chongqing
questions.explanation: Stilwell believed Jiang was avoiding offensives against Japan and keeping troops to blockade the communists. Supporters of Jiang reply that China had already suffered huge losses and lacked the means for major offensives.

questions.stem: Which feature of Mao's wartime leadership helped the CCP grow from the late 1930s?
options: ordering an immediate seizure of all landlords' land in every single area that the party controlled
moving the CCP's headquarters to Chongqing so it could share power with the Nationalists
presenting the CCP as patriotic resisters while using moderate policies to win peasant support
seeking a separate peace with Japan in order to concentrate all forces against the KMT
questions.explanation: Mao combined patriotic resistance with rent and interest reduction rather than land confiscation, which kept landlords and peasants in a broad front. Party membership and the communist armies grew greatly by 1945.

questions.stem: During the Yan'an period, the CCP's Rectification Movement of 1942-1944:
options: invited Nationalist officials to Yan'an to help reform the communist government
opened elections for party leadership to all residents of the communist base areas
expelled Mao from the Politburo for his failures in the war against Japan
used study, criticism and self-criticism, and coercion, to enforce loyalty to Mao's line
questions.explanation: Party members studied set documents, confessed errors and were pressured to conform, while Kang Sheng's security apparatus persecuted suspected spies. The movement made Mao's thought the party's orthodoxy.

questions.stem: Why was the Yan'an period socially significant for the CCP's later success?
options: It developed a model of rural government, mass mobilisation and moderate reform that won support
It was the first time the CCP ruled over a large city, which gave it industrial experience
It ended the CCP's links with peasants as the party focused on training urban workers
It led the CCP to give up guerrilla warfare and rely on Soviet tanks and aircraft
questions.explanation: In Yan'an and other base areas the CCP practised rent reduction, local elections, literacy campaigns and production drives, which historians such as Mark Selden called the 'Yan'an Way'. Yan'an was a small rural town, and guerrilla methods continued.

questions.stem: Edgar Snow's Red Star Over China (1937) and the American 'Dixie Mission' of 1944 were significant because they:
options: gave Western audiences a favourable picture of the communists and their base areas
proved that the CCP was controlled directly by Soviet officers sent from Moscow
persuaded the US government to cut off all aid to Jiang Jieshi's government in 1944
were written by Nationalist officials to warn the world about communist methods
questions.explanation: Snow, an American journalist, visited the communist base in 1936 and portrayed its leaders sympathetically, and US observers sent to Yan'an in 1944 reported on communist discipline and popular support. US aid continued to go to the Nationalists.

questions.stem: The mission of US General George Marshall to China in 1945-1947 aimed to:
options: arrange the handover of Manchuria to the Soviet Union in return for peace
persuade Jiang Jieshi to resign and hand power to the communists peacefully
negotiate a ceasefire and a coalition government between the KMT and the CCP
lead American troops in an invasion of the communist base areas in the north
questions.explanation: Marshall brokered a short-lived truce in early 1946, but mistrust on both sides wrecked it, and full civil war broke out. He left China in January 1947.

questions.stem: Which factor gave the CCP an advantage in Manchuria at the start of the Civil War?
options: Soviet forces that had occupied Manchuria allowed the CCP access to captured Japanese weapons
The USA handed the region's cities to the communists to prevent a Soviet takeover
The Nationalist army refused to enter Manchuria because it had no strategic value
The Japanese army in Manchuria joined the communists and fought on their side to 1949
questions.explanation: The Soviet army entered Manchuria in August 1945 and, before withdrawing in 1946, let CCP forces move in and obtain large stocks of Japanese arms. Manchuria, with its industry, became the CCP's key base under Lin Biao.

questions.stem: Which change in CCP tactics during the Civil War best explains its victories in 1948-1949?
options: A reliance on bombing the Nationalist cities with aircraft supplied by the Soviet Union
A shift from guerrilla war to large conventional campaigns once its armies were strong enough
A shift from conventional battles to guerrilla war after it lost Manchuria to the Nationalists
A decision to hold every city at all costs rather than give up any ground to the enemy
questions.explanation: The CCP gave up territory, including Yan'an in 1947, to preserve its forces, then moved to mobile and conventional warfare. The Liaoshen, Huaihai and Pingjin campaigns of 1948-1949 destroyed the main Nationalist armies.

questions.stem: The Huaihai Campaign of 1948-1949 was significant because:
options: the CCP destroyed major Nationalist armies north of the Yangtze, opening the way south
the Nationalists recaptured Yan'an and forced the communists to retreat north into Manchuria
the Japanese army returned to China and defeated both the KMT and the communists
Jiang Jieshi won his most important victory and drove the communists out of Beijing
questions.explanation: The communist victory in the Huaihai Campaign in east-central China, with huge Nationalist losses and surrenders, was decisive. The PLA crossed the Yangtze in April 1949 and took Nanjing.

questions.stem: How did hyperinflation in the late 1940s help the CCP win the Civil War?
options: It made communist-controlled areas poorer, so peasants there turned against the CCP
It allowed the Nationalists to pay their soldiers generously, which raised their morale
It forced the USA to cancel China's debts, so the Nationalists could buy more weapons
It ruined the urban middle class and civil servants and destroyed confidence in the Nationalists
questions.explanation: Prices rose so fast that savings and salaries became worthless, and the 1948 gold yuan reform failed. Groups that had supported the Nationalists lost faith in the government, and soldiers were badly paid.

questions.stem: Which CCP policy did most to win peasant recruits during the Civil War?
options: paying peasants in American dollars for every recruit who joined the army
exempting peasants from all military service in return for paying high rents
redistributing landlords' land to poor peasants in the areas it controlled
promising peasants that their land would be collectivised at once after victory
questions.explanation: From 1946, and under the Outline Land Law of 1947, the CCP confiscated and redistributed land, giving peasants a stake in communist victory and a reason to join the PLA. Collectivisation was not announced until the 1950s.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the Nationalists lost the Civil War more than the communists won it. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: The communists had more aircraft, tanks and foreign aid than the Nationalists throughout the war
The Nationalists were supported by most peasants, but the CCP had the backing of the landlords
The CCP won a national election in 1948 that forced the Nationalists to hand over the government
Corruption, inflation, poor morale and mass defections weakened Nationalist armies before major defeats
questions.explanation: Many Nationalist units surrendered or defected whole, often with their American equipment, and the government had lost credibility. The Nationalists in fact began the war with more troops and better equipment, and there was no such election.

questions.stem: After the communist victory, Jiang Jieshi and the Nationalist government withdrew in 1949 to:
options: Taiwan
Hong Kong
Manchuria
Tibet
questions.explanation: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949, and the Nationalists moved their government to Taiwan in December 1949, where it continued as the Republic of China. Hong Kong was a British colony.
